title: Distributed Tracing
subtitle: Propagating W3C Trace Context across RPC and message boundaries to reconstruct end-to-end request waterfalls.
keyTakeaways: In a distributed microservice architecture, individual server logs are useless without a correlated Trace ID that links operations across service hops.
The W3C `traceparent` standard provides an interoperable HTTP header format for propagating Trace ID, Parent Span ID, and sampling flags across networks.
Tail-Based Sampling collects 100% of spans in an in-memory buffer and retains only traces that experienced errors or high p99 latency, drastically cutting storage costs.

sections.heading: Traces, Spans, and W3C Traceparent Propagation
sections.body: When an end-user request crosses 15 independent microservices and two Kafka topics before returning an error, searching isolated application log files is an exercise in futility. Distributed tracing models a request's path as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of Spans.
bullets: Trace ID: A globally unique 128-bit identifier assigned to the user request at the edge gateway that remains constant across every subsequent service hop.
Span: Represents an individual unit of contiguous work (e.g., executing an HTTP call or SQL query), recording start time, duration, tags, and error logs.

W3C Traceparent Header: The modern OpenTelemetry standard format: `00-{trace-id}-{parent-span-id}-{trace-flags}`. Passing this header in outbound HTTP requests and Kafka message headers preserves the causal waterfall tree across heterogeneous platforms.

sections.heading: Head-Based vs Tail-Based Sampling
sections.body: At 100,000 requests per second, storing 100% of distributed trace spans produces petabytes of telemetry data, creating millions of dollars in observability tooling bills.
bullets: Head-Based Sampling: The edge gateway makes a probabilistic sampling decision upfront (e.g., sample 1% of requests). The decision (`trace-flags = 01`) propagates down the entire call tree. Problem: rare production errors occurring in the un-sampled 99% are permanently lost.

Tail-Based Sampling: The OpenTelemetry Collector buffers all trace spans in memory for 30 seconds. Once the entire trace completes, the collector inspects the outcome. If any span recorded an HTTP 5xx error or exceeded the p95 latency threshold, the trace is retained 100%; healthy, fast traces are discarded.

tradeOffs.pros: Captures 100% of production errors and latency anomalies; eliminates wasted storage on normal fast requests.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires running OpenTelemetry Collector fleets with sufficient memory to buffer in-flight spans across nodes.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-scale production microservice platforms processing tens of thousands of requests per second.

tradeOffs.pros: Zero memory buffering in telemetry collectors; simple edge gateway configuration.
tradeOffs.cons: Routinely misses intermittent bugs, rare error spikes, and edge-case tail latency regressions.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Low-budget early stage architectures with uniform traffic patterns.

interviewTip: In observability discussions, highlight Tail-Based Sampling: 'At 100k QPS, storing every trace span is cost-prohibitive. We use OpenTelemetry with Tail-Based Sampling in our collector fleet: spans are buffered in memory until the request completes, and we only retain traces that contained errors or breached our p95 latency threshold of 200ms.'
